summaryHeading: Was it "no license" or "license not on you"? The difference decides the case
summary: Driving without a valid license is a Class C misdemeanor under Texas Transportation Code 521.021. It is fine-only, but a conviction stays on record and can complicate getting or renewing a Texas license later.

If you have a license but didn't have it on you, that is a different, lesser charge ("failure to display") that courts in El Paso County generally dismiss once you show the license was valid on the date of the stop.
For drivers who were truly unlicensed — including many drivers from Ciudad Juárez and teens on permits — we work for deferred disposition, which ends in a dismissal instead of a conviction.

sections.heading: Two Different Tickets: No License vs. Failure to Display
paragraphs: El Paso officers write two charges that sound alike but are very different. The first is no driver's license — Transportation Code 521.021 — meaning you were driving without ever having been issued a valid license, or your license had lapsed. The second is failure to display: you hold a valid license but left it at home, in another purse, or in the truck you weren't driving that day. Officers frequently write the heavier charge on the roadside because they can't verify anything at 11 p.m. on Alameda Avenue.

If your license was valid on the date of the stop, your case is usually straightforward. We obtain your driving record, show the prosecutor that the license existed, and ask for a dismissal. Courts in El Paso County treat this as a paperwork problem, and it is generally resolved without you appearing. The key is not to pay the ticket first — paying it is a guilty plea to a charge you never committed.

If you genuinely had no license, the stakes are higher and the strategy is different, which is what the rest of this page is about. Not sure which charge is on your citation, or whether it was filed at all? Use the free ticket and warrant lookup and we'll tell you.

sections.heading: Why a No Driver's License Conviction Hurts More Than the Fine
paragraphs: The fine itself is small: a Class C misdemeanor, capped at $200 for a first offense, plus court costs set by the court. The real damage comes later. When you apply for a Texas license at the DPS office on Hondo Pass or Gateway Boulevard, the examiner sees the conviction. Unresolved tickets and OMNI holds from unpaid cases block the application outright, and repeat offenses carry escalating penalties.

That is why deferred disposition matters so much on these tickets. Under Code of Criminal Procedure art. 45A.302 (formerly art. 45.051), the judge defers a finding of guilt for a period the court sets, commonly 90 to 180 days; if you stay out of trouble (and, in these cases, often if you actually get licensed), the case is dismissed and there is never a conviction. Many El Paso judges will condition the deferral on proof that you obtained a license or a learner permit — which turns the ticket into a push to fix the underlying problem rather than a mark that follows you. Our page on deferred adjudication and defensive driving explains how the deferral period works.

sections.heading: Drivers From Juárez, Foreign Licenses and New Residents
paragraphs: No city in Texas sees more no-license tickets involving a border than El Paso. Tens of thousands of people cross the Paso del Norte, Ysleta–Zaragoza and Bridge of the Americas crossings every day, and a Chihuahua license is generally valid for a visitor driving in Texas. The problem arises when an officer decides the driver actually lives in El Paso — a Texas address on the insurance, a child enrolled in an EPISD school, a job at an east-side warehouse — and treats the Mexican license as no license at all. Texas generally expects new residents to get a Texas license within 90 days of moving here.

These cases turn on facts: where you live, how long you've been here, and what documents you can show. Our office handles them regularly, and we generally ask for a deferred disposition or a reduced charge that doesn't require you to appear and doesn't produce a conviction. We also see Fort Bliss families, students at UTEP with licenses from other states, and workers who moved from New Mexico and never switched over. Se habla español — tell us the story and we'll tell you the options.

sections.heading: Teen Drivers, Learner Permits and Provisional Licenses
paragraphs: A 16-year-old with a learner permit who drives alone, or a 17-year-old on a provisional license out after midnight with three friends in the car, can be cited under the same no-license statute or for violating permit restrictions. For a teenager, a conviction is especially costly: it can delay the move from permit to full license and gives the family's insurance carrier a reason to re-rate the whole policy.

We handle these tickets with the parent, not just the teen. The usual goal is deferred disposition, sometimes paired with a driver education requirement the judge is happy to see, so that nothing goes on the young driver's record. Depending on the court, a defensive driving option may also be available on companion tickets like speeding.

faqs.q: What is the penalty for driving without a license in Texas?
faqs.a: A first offense under Transportation Code 521.021 is a Class C misdemeanor — a fine of up to $200 plus court costs, no jail. The bigger consequence is the conviction on your record, which can complicate getting a Texas license later. Repeat offenses carry heavier penalties.

faqs.q: I have a license but didn't have it with me. Will the ticket be dismissed?
faqs.a: If your license was valid on the date of the stop, Texas law treats that as a defense, and we show the prosecutor your driving record and ask for a dismissal. Don't pay the ticket first — that is a guilty plea to a charge you didn't commit.

faqs.q: Is a Mexican driver's license valid in El Paso?
faqs.a: For a visitor, generally yes. The dispute usually comes when an officer believes the driver actually lives in El Paso and should have a Texas license. Those cases depend on your residency facts, and we generally ask for deferred disposition so there is no conviction.

faqs.q: Can I get a Texas license if I have a no-license ticket pending?
faqs.a: An unresolved ticket, especially one that has gone to warrant or an OMNI hold, generally blocks a license application until it is cleared. Resolving the ticket through our office — ideally with a deferred disposition — clears the path. See our OMNI hold removal page if a hold is already in place.

faqs.q: Will deferred disposition keep the ticket off my record?
faqs.a: Deferred disposition under art. 45A.302 ends in a dismissal if you complete the deferral period, so there is no conviction and nothing reported as one. Some El Paso judges require proof that you obtained a license or permit as a condition.

faqs.q: My teenager was cited for driving alone on a learner permit. What now?
faqs.a: Hire us before the appearance date and don't pay the ticket. We generally work for deferred disposition so the permit violation never becomes a conviction that delays the full license or raises the family's insurance.
